A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DiscoverLLM with the same authors, core framework, and main experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated experiments across three domains, generalization and safety evaluations, and a 75-participant user study, including results in Appendices B–D.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds simulator robustness experiments, independent benchmark evaluations, a reward ablation, human intent-tree validation, and analysis of the user-study conversations.

M1.justification: The proposed hierarchy construction, discovery-state updates, combined discovery and efficiency reward, and SFT/DPO/GRPO framework remain unchanged. Appendix A and the eleven prompts are unchanged. Alternative simulator configurations and discovery-only DPO are introduced as experimental ablations, without replacing the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix B.9 adds clarification-oriented document editing on 50 Medium articles and question answering on 400 AmbigNQ plus 400 NQ-Open questions. These extend evaluation beyond intent discovery in artifact creation to users with formed but unexpressed goals and ambiguous factual questions. The original domains, generalization tasks, and safety benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Base, Prompted Base, and CollabLLM remain the external comparators, and the new independent benchmarks reuse that set. Table 11 adds a discovery-only offline-DPO variant as an internal ablation comparator against full-reward DPO, constituting a limited addition to comparison methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include controlled simulator ablations on 25 artifacts per domain, eight-turn document editing with character-level BLEU, and optional clarification followed by F1/answer-recall evaluation on 800 questions. Human validation uses 314 intent pairs and three raters per pair; conversation annotation combines LLM screening with manual verification. Section 6 also corrects the reported satisfaction cutoff from 7 to 8, without evidence of rerunning the user study.

E4.justification: v2 adds four simulator robustness tests: two alternative backbones, removal of single-dimension focus, and increased tangential probability. It also adds a reward-component ablation, human validation and error analysis of intent trees, and checks of monotonicity and dimension-switching assumptions in all 75 user-study conversations. These investigate central validity and mechanism questions absent from v1.

E5.justification: Appendix B.8 newly specifies that seeds are held fixed across simulator-ablation conditions. This is limited additional seed-control documentation. Three-trial averaging was already reported in v1; v2 does not establish increased repetitions for retained experiments or introduce confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Main benchmark and retained appendix results are unchanged, but Tables 4–5 and 8–12 add substantial findings. These include BLEU 0.274 versus Base's 0.239, Ambig F1 0.202 versus CollabLLM's 0.197, and assumption violations in 4/75 and 11/75 conversations. Section 6 corrects Base's satisfaction percentage from 78% to 80% alongside the changed cutoff; the underlying Figure 5 is unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, hierarchy definition, state-transition equations, reward functions, and formal assumptions are retained. Section 2.3 rewrites their explanation, while Appendix C.1 empirically examines existing assumptions rather than changing them. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: formalizing intent discovery, constructing a hierarchical user simulator, and training assistants to balance exploration and execution. Claims about performance, efficiency, generalization, and human satisfaction remain substantively unchanged; the additions supply further supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of simulator robustness, hierarchy errors, and observed assumption violations. It explains how excessive diversity can disrupt technical-writing conventions and attributes discovery performance primarily to Rd while Re controls verbosity. Appendix B.10 explicitly qualifies this attribution because both reward variants inherit conversation contexts generated under the full reward.

D1.justification: v2 adds a title-page project link and concrete details for the new experiments, including alternative simulator model names, tangential probability 0.75, and reward-ablation preference relabeling with shared trajectories. Existing training hyperparameters, synthesis-cost information, simulator implementation description, and prompts are retained.

R1.justification: The Almeda et al. (2024) DreamSheets reference is removed, and its related-work citation becomes an unresolved question mark. The remaining research positioning is largely unchanged. New evaluations engage more directly with the already-cited CollabLLM and clarification frameworks without redefining the paper's novelty.

P1.justification: v2 tightens Section 2.3, makes scattered grammatical and cross-reference corrections, expands Section 5.3 with labeled paragraphs, and adds appendix subsections and acknowledgements. Conference front matter replaces the preprint notice. The established narrative and section organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: New Tables 4–5 and 8–12 provide dedicated displays for hierarchy statistics and validation, simulator robustness, independent benchmarks, reward ablation, and assumption checks. This substantially expands the empirical presentation. Existing figures and tables are retained, with limited resizing, relocation, and renumbering rather than replacement.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central validation gap: whether gains depend on its custom simulator and unverified intent hierarchies. Alternative simulators, independent benchmarks, human tree validation, and conversation-level assumption checks substantially strengthen the empirical foundation. The reward ablation transparently acknowledges shared trajectories. Some reporting defects remain or are introduced: Table 8's tangential column shows 53.7 versus the best baseline's 50.8, implying a 2.9-point gap rather than the printed 3.4. These limited defects do not outweigh the broader validation gains.
